# Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?

Won Seok Jang^(†) Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell
Correspondence:[WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu](mailto:WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu)
   Harry Bhaskar Joshi^(†) Affiliation: University of Massachusetts
Lowell
Correspondence:[WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu](mailto:WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu)
   Hong Yu Affiliation: University of Massachusetts Lowell
Correspondence:[WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu](mailto:WonSeok_Jang@student.uml.edu)

###### Abstract

Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that
improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system.
However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated
reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration
reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured
in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer.
We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent
topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring
hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the
rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task
metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower
hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than
another. The effect differs by model: of the $`36`$ model–system–task
comparisons, $`12`$ are large enough to resolve — four decreases and
eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and
the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or
the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with
this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which
collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most,
does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration
redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what
they cannot.

## 1 Introduction

Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used on clinical problems that
a single model handles poorly. Panels of specialist agents improve
diagnostic accuracy [Kim et al. (2024)](#bib.bib1), structured
collaboration raises performance on dementia assessment [Li et al.
(2025a)](#bib.bib2) and on both rare and common disease [Li et al.
(2025b)](#bib.bib38), and surveys describe a fast-growing design space
built on the same premise [Tran et al. (2025)](#bib.bib7). This premise
is intuitive: more heads catch more errors. If multiple agents read a
case and reconcile their views, the mistakes any one of them makes
should not survive the group.

However, this research establishes that collaboration improves answers.
It does not establish that collaboration produces fewer hallucinations.
Most evaluations report a task metric and read an improvement as
evidence of a more trustworthy system [Kim et al. (2024)](#bib.bib1);
[Li et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib2), yet a system can select the right option
for stated reasons that the source does not support [Yang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib35); [Kalai et al. (2025)](#bib.bib5). In the clinic
that gap is the risk rather than a technicality. A clinician acts on the
stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so an unsupported claim
inside a rationale is itself the harm [Gallifant et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib36); [Wang et al. (2023a)](#bib.bib37). There is also
reason to expect collaboration to make this worse rather than better,
since audits of medical multi-agent systems report unsupported findings
propagating through the group as false consensus [Zhu et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib25). Few studies measure hallucination inside the
rationale and report it alongside the task metric for the same
generation.

Therefore, we conduct an analytical study that measures both task
performance and hallucination in the same generation. We evaluate four
systems — a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies — on
four models and three clinical tasks, and we measure task performance
(accuracy, label-$`F_{1}`$) alongside the hallucination rate. For the
sub-types we take the factuality and faithfulness axes of [Huang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib16). Hallucination is scored inside the rationale each
system generates: the rationale is decomposed into atomic claims
following [Min and others (2023)](#bib.bib22), and we report a per-case
claim rate for each sub-type — factual contradiction and factual
fabrication on the factuality axis, contextual and logical inconsistency
on the faithfulness axis. Because every multi-agent topology works by
having a model revise text written by instances of itself, we also ask
whether collaboration’s effect depends on how well a model revises its
own output. We report three findings.

- •
  Performance and hallucination correlate negatively across models, but
  not within one. Higher-performing models hallucinate less; the
  relationship disappears when only the topology varies.
- •
  Collaboration has no fixed effect on hallucination; the effect has a
  direction, and the direction is conditioned on the model.
  Collaboration is neither a safety improvement one can assume nor one
  that is simply unavailable — it amplifies hallucination for some
  models and genuinely reduces it for one. Further analysis with scaling
  and ablation studies supports this.
- •
  Self-correction capability tracks the effect. Shown its own errors,
  every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination. The
  model that gains the most from this correction is the one
  collaboration helps, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, which collaboration
  harms most, does not reduce its hallucination at all.

## 2 Background and Related Work

#### Does collaboration reduce hallucination?

The literature answers both ways. One line holds that it does.
Multi-agent debate was introduced in part as a remedy: several instances
of a model critique one another’s reasoning, and the resulting answers
are reported to be more factual than a single model’s [Du et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib12). The same intuition — that errors are idiosyncratic
and agreement filters them out — underlies pooling independent
attempts [Wang et al. (2023b)](#bib.bib8); [Li et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib9), layered proposer stacks [Wang et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib13), medical specialist panels [Kim et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib1), and collaborative abstention, where a group
withholds answers no member is confident in [Feng et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib19).

The other line holds that it does not, or that the gain is an artifact.
Under a matched sampling budget, a single model with self-consistency
recovers much of debate’s reported advantage, suggesting the benefit
came from drawing more samples rather than from agents talking to each
other [Tran and Kiela (2026)](#bib.bib11); debate has been found to
underperform simpler baselines [Smit et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23); and
audits of medical multi-agent systems report the opposite of
error-filtering, with unsupported findings propagating through the group
as false consensus [Zhu et al. (2026)](#bib.bib25).

#### Collaboration as self-correction.

Each multi-agent topology contains a step in which a model reads
responses that have already been written and produces a revised version.
For example, a debater updates after reading its peers, a moderator
keeps what the panel supports, and a refiner re-answers over the
proposals. This operation could be viewed as self-correction, where a
model revises an output given feedback on it [Madaan et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib14); [Kamoi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib32). In multi-agent
collaboration, the text under revision is the model’s own, since every
agent runs on the same model [Du et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12); [Kim et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib1). Self-correction depends on the model: models often
fail to find their own errors yet can repair them once the errors are
located [Tyen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29), and without reliable feedback,
correction rarely helps [Huang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib30). If
collaboration acts through the same step, its effect on hallucination
should depend on the model in the same way.

#### Hallucination taxonomies.

Several schemes organize language-model hallucination: intrinsic versus
extrinsic [Ji et al. (2023)](#bib.bib24), input-, context- and
fact-conflicting [Zhang et al. (2023)](#bib.bib17), and finer-grained
clinical error types [Kim et al. (2025)](#bib.bib3). We adopt the
two-axis taxonomy (factuality and faithfulness) of [Huang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib16) because it cuts at the level of what a generation is
answerable to, which keeps it simple while encompassing the schemes
above.

Factuality hallucination departs from established world knowledge,
independent of any source given to the model. It divides into _factual
contradiction_, where a statement contradicts verifiable knowledge, and
_factual fabrication_, where a statement has no basis in established
knowledge and cannot be checked against it at all. A faithfulness
hallucination departs from something the model was given, and divides
into _instruction inconsistency_, where the output ignores what was
asked of it; _contextual inconsistency_, where it contradicts or is
unsupported by the supplied source; and _logical inconsistency_, where
the reasoning contradicts itself regardless of any external reference.

#### Collaboration topologies.

Work on multi-agent design describes these systems along two
complementary axes. The first is organizational: [Tran et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib7) classify systems as Centralized, Decentralized or
Hierarchical according to where control over inter-agent communication
resides. The second is functional: [Zhou et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10)
treat a system as an ordered pipeline of building blocks and search over
their compositions; three blocks recur — Aggregate, parallel proposers
whose outputs are pooled by an aggregation operator; Reflect, a verifier
that critiques or refines a prior output; and Debate, fully connected
multi-round exchange between peers. Both are accounts of _structure_,
and both evaluate structure against a task metric; neither discusses
what a given composition does to the content a system generates.

## 3 Experimental Setup

### 3.1 Topology Types

Figure 1: The four systems. Every seat holds the same model, so the
systems differ only in the number of agents, their prompts and how they
are wired; orange marks the agent that commits to the final answer. Each
produces a rationale alongside its answer, and it is that rationale the
hallucination measures score.

We compare four systems
(Figure [1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Topology Types ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")):
a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent configurations built from
the Aggregate, Reflect, and Debate blocks of [Zhou et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10). Every multi-agent system ends in an explicit
_aggregator role_ that sees the original query — including the source
document and the answer options — together with the sub-agents’ outputs,
and commits to the final answer. In every multi-agent system, then, a
model reads text produced by instances of itself and decides what to
keep; we return to this step in
§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Self-Correction Capability and Multi-Agent Collaboration ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

#### SLS (single-LLM system)

A single LLM answers the item end-to-end, with no intermediate steps or
refinement.

#### Panel

Three specialist agents answer in parallel and a moderator synthesizes a
single final answer, adopting only conclusions that at least two of the
three specialists independently support and discarding claims raised by
a lone specialist. The design adapts the specialist-panel-with-moderator
pattern of MDAgents [Kim et al. (2024)](#bib.bib1) to a fixed panel
size.

#### Debate

Three peer agents exchange responses over two rounds of fully connected
debate, each updating its answer after observing the others’; a final
aggregator then synthesizes the debated positions into one answer. The
design follows multi-agent debate [Du et al. (2023)](#bib.bib12).

#### Hierarchical

Three proposer agents independently generate candidate responses; a
second layer of three refiner agents re-answers conditioned on the
concatenation of all first-layer responses; a single aggregator then
synthesizes the final answer. The design adapts the layered proposer
stack of Mixture-of-Agents [Wang et al. (2024)](#bib.bib13); [Chen et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib15).

Figure 2: Hallucination taxonomy used for our analysis: factuality
hallucination and faithfulness hallucination.

### 3.2 Hallucination Evaluation

Figure 3: How a rationale becomes a hallucination rate: decompose, judge
each claim, judge each pair. Grey marks a label the judge assigns but
the paper does not report.

We measure the two axes of hallucination
(§[2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"))
inside the system’s own generated rationale
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 Hallucination Evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Hierarchical ‣ 3.1 Topology Types ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
illustrates the four sub-types we report. Every rate we report is formed
the same way: within one rationale we take the share of its claims
carrying the label, and the reported number is the mean of that share
over rationales, which is the _claim rate per case_. A task’s overall
hallucination rate counts a claim that carries any of the task’s
reported labels. Scoring uses an LLM as a judge (gemma-4-31B-it [Gemma
Team (2026)](#bib.bib27) from Google). Each rationale is first
decomposed into _atomic claims_ — self-contained single-fact statements
with pronouns resolved and negation preserved — following the
atomic-fact procedure of FActScore [Min and others (2023)](#bib.bib22);
near-duplicate claims are removed. Each task’s reference is given in
Appendix Table [C](#A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1 "MedExpQA retrieval. ‣ Appendix C Task Definitions ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

#### Factuality.

Each claim is checked against what the task supplies — the case, the
answer options, and the human-written gold explanation — and labeled
supported, contradicted, or unverifiable. To make the evaluation of
factuality hallucination more complete, every claim the supplied
reference leaves open is then checked against an external corpus of
$`346{,}691`$ medical passages (MedRAG [Xiong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib42)
textbooks and StatPearls), retrieved with BM25 at $`k{=}20`$ and judged
by the same judge against the retrieved evidence; no system in the study
has access to this corpus. The two hallucination labels are
reference-relative proxies for the categories of
§[2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"):
a claim either reference refutes is counted as a _factual
contradiction_, and one that neither can support or refute as a _factual
fabrication_.

#### Faithfulness.

We measure two sub-types. _Contextual inconsistency_ applies the same
claim-level procedure with the provided source — the discharge note(s),
or the brief hospital course and summary — as the reference, labeling
each claim supported, contradicted, or not-in-context. We report the
contradiction rate. Following [Johnson-Laird et al. (2004)](#bib.bib40),
we judge _logical inconsistency_ by whether a rationale contradicts
itself, with the source document in view. The procedure is a pipeline in
two steps. The two claims of every pair are first checked against each
other — can both be true of the same patient and the same admission? —
and every pair that conflicts is then resolved with the source document
and the full rationale restored, receiving its final label of
contradiction, compatible or unclear. Only contradiction is counted. We
report the share of a rationale’s claims that take part in a
contradiction.

#### LLM-as-a-judge validation.

We validate the judge against human annotation. Two of the authors
independently annotated blind stratified samples — $`150`$ MedExpQA
claims for factuality, $`100`$ claims for contextual inconsistency and
$`100`$ claim pairs for logical inconsistency. Following [Chung et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib26), we take human–human agreement as the reference:
judge–human agreement is comparable to it on all three measures, under
either Cohen’s $`\kappa`$ or Gwet’s AC1 [Gwet (2008)](#bib.bib41), and
exceeds it under both coefficients on factuality and contextual
inconsistency (Appendix
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix D Judge Validation Details ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"));
the annotation instructions are given in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Judge Validation Details ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

### 3.3 Models

We use four models, GPT-5.4-mini [Singh et al. (2025)](#bib.bib18),
DeepSeek-V4.1-flash [DeepSeek-AI et al. (2026)](#bib.bib31),
Qwen3-32B [Qwen Team (2025)](#bib.bib20), and
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct [Grattafiori et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4), chosen to
span a range of sizes and benchmark performance. Reasoning modes are
disabled. All but GPT-5.4-mini are open-weight.

### 3.4 Benchmarks

We evaluate on three clinical tasks, summarized in
Appendix Table [C](#A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1 "MedExpQA retrieval. ‣ Appendix C Task Definitions ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").
We chose these three because each supplies a _verifiable gold label_, so
that correctness can be judged objectively, and a context against which
a system’s stated reasoning, not only its final answer, can be assessed.
Every system is prompted to produce a rationale, and the rationale is
evaluated for hallucination.

#### MedExpQA

[Alonso et al. (2024)](#bib.bib28) is a medical exam-style
multiple-choice benchmark with a human-written explanation of the
correct option. Each claim in the rationale is judged against that
explanation and against passages retrieved from our own corpus
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Hallucination Evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?");
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Task Definitions ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
For this dataset, we measure the factuality sub-types: factual
contradiction and factual fabrication.

#### EHRNoteQA

[Kweon and others (2024)](#bib.bib21) asks a question about a specific
patient’s discharge note(s), with the note(s) supplied. A claim is
judged against them. Here and on Hallucinations-MIMIC-DI (MIMIC-DI) we
measure the faithfulness sub-types, contextual and logical
inconsistency.

#### Hallucinations-MIMIC-DI

[Hegselmann et al. (2025)](#bib.bib6) pairs each brief hospital course
with a discharge summary, and the system’s task is to work as a
detector, flagging every unsupported span _and stating the reason_. The
task metric scores the flagged spans against medical-expert gold spans,
while the stated reasons are scored for hallucination.

We run every combination of the four systems and four models on all
three tasks, $`200`$ items each, and score each generation with both the
task metric and the hallucination measures. Brackets are $`95\%`$
bootstrap confidence intervals over items; where two systems are
compared on the same items we use a paired bootstrap. Each cell is a
single generation run, and every interval uses at least $`2{,}000`$
resamples.

## 4 Experiments

Figure 4: Task performance (top) and hallucination rate (bottom), by
model and system.

### 4.1 Performance and Hallucination

Across models, task score and hallucination are strongly anti-correlated
— $`r=-0.82`$ on MedExpQA, $`-0.97`$ on EHRNoteQA and $`-0.89`$ on
detection — so better-performing models tend to hallucinate less
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
However, within a fixed model, where only the topology varies, the
relationship does not hold: the correlation over a model’s four systems
ranges from $`-0.82`$ to $`+0.94`$, with no consistent sign. On MedExpQA
GPT-5.4-mini hallucinates at $`0.153`$ as a single agent against
$`0.297`$ for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and no topology moves either model
more than $`0.053`$ from its own baseline. Collaboration does change
hallucination in some cells, and the direction depends on the model.
When each multi-agent cell is compared with its own single-agent
baseline, $`12`$ of the $`36`$ comparisons have a $`95\%`$ interval
excluding zero: four decreases, all for GPT-5.4-mini, and eight
increases, spread over the other three models. The split is consistent
with the sign being a property of the model, which the experiments below
probe more directly.

Collaboration does tend to help on the task: a multi-agent system beats
its single-agent baseline in $`23`$ of the $`36`$ comparisons, and the
best cell on each task is a multi-agent system — DeepSeek-V4.1-flash
reaches $`0.895`$ on MedExpQA and $`0.950`$ on EHRNoteQA against
$`0.875`$ and $`0.935`$ as a single agent, and GPT-5.4-mini reaches a
label-$`F_{1}`$ of $`0.497`$ on detection against $`0.415`$.
Collaboration’s effect on hallucination does not follow. In
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"),
each model’s multi-agent systems stay close to its single-agent value
while the models sit far apart, so a multi-agent system cannot be
assumed to be the safer choice. The cross-model correlation is strong
but not deterministic: DeepSeek-V4.1-flash outscores GPT-5.4-mini on
both multiple-choice tasks yet hallucinates more on MedExpQA ($`0.203`$
against $`0.153`$).

Figure 5: Factuality hallucination on MedExpQA, by factual contradiction
and factual fabrication.

Figure 6: Faithfulness hallucination, by sub-type and task.

### 4.2 Hallucination Category Analysis

#### Factuality.

Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Performance and Hallucination ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
separates factual contradiction from factual fabrication on MedExpQA.
Only GPT-5.4-mini improves on both: factual contradiction falls from
$`0.042`$ as a single agent to $`0.034`$ under the Hierarchical system,
and fabrication from $`0.110`$ to $`0.096`$ under the Panel.
DeepSeek-V4.1-flash splits the two, and the split is informative —
factual contradiction falls from $`0.056`$ to $`0.049`$ under the Panel
while fabrication rises from $`0.147`$ to $`0.174`$, so the same
manipulation that removes claims a reference can refute adds claims no
reference can reach. For Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct every
multi-agent arm sits above its single-agent baseline on both sub-types.
For every model, the topology that is best on factual contradiction is
not the best on fabrication, so no topology is reliably better; Debate
is the worst arm on both sub-types for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.

#### Faithfulness.

Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Performance and Hallucination ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
shows the two sub-types behaving differently. Contextual inconsistency
moves very little: every model’s multi-agent arms sit close to its own
single-agent baseline, above it as often as below, with no arm clearly
ahead. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct’s Debate is again the worst arm, on both
tasks, exactly as in factuality.

Logical inconsistency shows the largest relative movement under
collaboration, and its direction again follows the model; it is also the
sub-type on which our judge agrees least with the annotators (Appendix
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Appendix D Judge Validation Details ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")),
so we interpret it with caution. On EHRNoteQA the single-agent rate is
lowest for GPT-5.4-mini and DeepSeek-V4.1-flash — $`0.007`$ and
$`0.005`$ of claims take part in a contradiction, against $`0.011`$ for
Qwen3-32B and $`0.015`$ for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct — and collaboration
moves the two ends in opposite directions. GPT-5.4-mini falls under all
three systems, to $`0.001`$ under the Hierarchical system ($`-0.006`$),
and DeepSeek-V4.1-flash falls under all three as well, by less
($`-0.002`$ under the Hierarchical system). By contrast,
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct climbs under all three, to $`0.029`$ ($`+0.014`$),
worst under the same system that helps GPT-5.4-mini most. Qwen3-32B sits
between, with little change. On MIMIC-DI detection the model ordering is
starker still — as single agents, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct shows $`0.061`$
against $`0.009`$ for GPT-5.4-mini — but the relative moves are smaller
than on EHRNoteQA. We return to this in
§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Self-Correction Capability and Multi-Agent Collaboration ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"):
the model whose logical inconsistency collaboration amplifies is also
the one that introduces the most new contradictions when it rewrites.

| EHRNoteQA contextual    | 0.042 | 0.023              | $`-0.019`$ |
| EHRNoteQA logical       | 0.010 | 0.003              | $`-0.007`$ |
| MIMIC-DI contextual     | 0.096 | 0.102              | $`+0.006`$ |
| MIMIC-DI logical        | 0.007 | 0.004              | $`-0.002`$ |
| _Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct_ |       |                    |            |
| MedExpQA contradiction  | 0.148 | 0.044              | $`-0.104`$ |
| MedExpQA fabrication    | 0.177 | 0.106              | $`-0.071`$ |
| EHRNoteQA contextual    | 0.129 | 0.030              | $`-0.099`$ |
| EHRNoteQA logical       | 0.024 | 0.002              | $`-0.023`$ |
| MIMIC-DI contextual     | 0.363 | 0.125              | $`-0.238`$ |
| MIMIC-DI logical        | 0.071 | 0.009              | $`-0.063`$ |

Table 2: Hallucination by sub-type when the aggregator alone is replaced
with GPT-5.4-mini, the proposal pool held fixed. Hierarchical system;
rows are each task’s sub-types, means over $`200`$ items. own: the
pool’s own model as aggregator, re-run under the same settings
(temperature $`=0`$).

We run two further manipulations: we scale each topology from three
agents to seven, changing nothing else
(Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Faithfulness. ‣ 4.2 Hallucination Category Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")),
and, in the Hierarchical system, we swap only the aggregator’s model,
reusing the saved proposer and refiner outputs
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?");
all pairings in Appendix
Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Pool and Aggregator Combinations ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).

Figure 7: Net change in hallucination after each model is shown its own
flagged claims (hallucination rate of the rewrite minus that of the
single agent, with $`95\%`$ bootstrap intervals). Green: interval
excludes zero. Levels in Appendix
Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Logical inconsistency. ‣ Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

Scaling has minimal effect, and what little it does depends on the axis.
Five of six factuality cells rise — no amount of conferring gives a
model a fact it does not have — and four of six faithfulness cells fall;
the mean changes are $`+0.005`$ and $`-0.002`$. Both effects are small
beside the gap between models, and only one of the $`12`$ intervals
excludes zero. Swapping the aggregator, by contrast, moves hallucination
across most of its observed range: for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct every
category falls, factual contradiction from $`0.148`$ to $`0.044`$ and
logical inconsistency on EHRNoteQA from $`0.024`$ to $`0.002`$ per claim
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
But the swapped system lands at about what its stronger member achieves
alone: with GPT-5.4-mini in the seat, factual contradiction is $`0.044`$
against GPT-5.4-mini’s single-agent $`0.042`$, and fabrication $`0.106`$
against $`0.110`$
(Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
Nor is the aggregator alone decisive — a Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
aggregator over a GPT-5.4-mini pool stays at $`0.031`$ in factual
contradiction on MedExpQA (Appendix
Table [5](#A5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix E Pool and Aggregator Combinations ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
Hallucination is high only when both positions are weak, and with
GPT-5.4-mini in either seat the system sits near GPT-5.4-mini’s own
level. Adding agents does little; what matters is the model that reads
them and decides what survives. The property that should matter, then,
is how well a model revises text once its errors are in view, whether
they are pointed out explicitly or only implied by disagreeing
proposals.

### 4.4 Self-Correction Capability and Multi-Agent Collaboration

If collaboration helps a model only insofar as the model can revise its
own output, then handing each model its own flagged errors should
separate the models the same way collaboration did [Liu et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib33); [Weng et al. (2023)](#bib.bib34). For every item
where the judge flagged a hallucination in a single-agent rationale, we
re-ran the same model on the same item with the flagged statements
appended to the prompt, each with its error type and, for MedExpQA, the
reference it failed against, and judged the rewrite as before
(Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?");
procedure in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).

Every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct uses the feedback, and none
becomes measurably worse. Averaged over the three sub-types where errors
are common, the reduction follows the same order as collaboration’s
effect
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
GPT-5.4-mini reduces factual contradiction by $`53\%`$ ($`0.042`$ to
$`0.020`$), fabrication by $`33\%`$ and contextual inconsistency by
$`22\%`$, and DeepSeek-V4.1-flash reduces all three by $`16`$–$`31\%`$.
Qwen3-32B reduces only factual contradiction ($`-19\%`$) and leaves
fabrication unchanged. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces none measurably:
factual contradiction falls by $`10\%`$, within noise, while fabrication
and contextual inconsistency rise by $`8\%`$ and $`6\%`$, also within
noise (Appendix
Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Logical inconsistency. ‣ Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
On logical inconsistency no model’s net change is distinguishable from
zero: every model removes most of the contradictions it is shown, but
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct introduces new ones at about twice the rate of the
others (Appendix
Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Logical inconsistency. ‣ Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).

This matches collaboration at its two ends. GPT-5.4-mini, the one model
collaboration improves, gains most from a correction;
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, whose hallucination collaboration amplifies most,
gains nothing, and the new contradictions it introduces match its rise
in logical inconsistency under collaboration
(Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4.1 Performance and Hallucination ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
The match is not exact: DeepSeek-V4.1-flash acts on a correction, yet
collaboration still raises its fabrication on MedExpQA
(Figure [5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.1 Performance and Hallucination ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
This is consistent with self-correction as the mechanism but does not
establish it: the experiment hands a model its errors, whereas
collaboration also requires finding them, and models find errors less
reliably than they repair them [Tyen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29). In
practice, an external verifier that flags hallucinated claims, as our
judge does here, could take over the finding step, but it would help
only a model that acts on what it is shown.

## 5 Conclusion

Multi-agent collaboration is not a hallucination remedy that can be
assumed. Across four systems, four models and three clinical tasks it
improves the task metric, but its effect on hallucination in the
rationale is set by the model: hallucination falls for the model that
gains most from a correction and rises most for the one that gains
least, and when models are mixed, hallucination stays high only if every
position is weak. Collaboration redistributes what its members can
already do; it does not supply what they cannot. An accuracy gain from
collaboration must not be reported as evidence of reduced hallucination
— in a clinical setting, where a person reads the justification and acts
on it, the two have to be measured separately.

## 6 Limitations and Future Directions

Here we discuss the limitations of this study and future research
directions.

First, the evidence rests on a handful of models and tasks. We evaluate
four models — one proprietary and three open-weight — on three tasks,
and the pattern may not hold for other models or clinical tasks. Second,
our four systems are representative but do not cover every existing
topology. A single agent, a panel, a debate and a two-layer hierarchy
cover the common building blocks of the multi-agent literature, but many
published systems combine them differently, add role specialization or
persistent memory, or route between agents adaptively. A system outside
our setting could behave differently. Third, our systems take no agentic
actions — no retrieval, no tool use, no interaction with an environment.
The scope here is collaboration among LLMs reasoning from what they are
given. A retrieval-augmented or tool-using multi-agent system is both
the more realistic deployment and the more interesting case for
hallucination, because grounding is then something the system can act on
rather than a fixed property of the model, and we regard it as the
natural next study. Fourth, factual contradiction and factual
fabrication are reference-relative proxies for the categories of [Huang
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib16), and fabrication is the weaker of the two. A
claim counts as contradicted when the gold explanation or a retrieved
passage refutes it, and as fabricated when neither can adjudicate it, so
fabrication depends on the reach of those references. The reported rate
is therefore an upper bound and less reliable than the contradiction
rate. Fifth, every system in our experiments uses a single backbone in
all of its seats, and only the roles of the agents vary; we mix
backbones only in the aggregator swap
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
Future work could study systems that mix backbones throughout. Sixth,
our self-correction experiment hands the flagged errors to a single
agent, not to a multi-agent system. It measures a property of the model,
whether it acts on its errors when shown them, which we compare with how
collaboration changes the same model. Every topology already contains a
revision step of this kind
(§[2](#S2 "2 Background and Related Work ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")),
so feedback given to a multi-agent system’s output would mix with the
revision inside collaboration, and we leave that combination to future
work. Seventh, two narrower points. Our logical-inconsistency measure is
built from pairs of a rationale’s claims that cannot both hold once read
against the source, so a rationale that considers and then rejects an
alternative can contribute to that count. It is also the sub-type whose
calls are hardest to make, since they often turn on whether two
differently worded claims refer to the same thing. And we study
_commission_ hallucination — unsupported content the system asserts —
not omission, a warranted finding the system fails to state, which
carries the opposite clinical risk. Finally, our results link a model’s
self-correction capability to the effect collaboration has on it, but
they do not establish that one causes the other. Future work could test
this directly, for example by varying how well a model acts on its
errors and measuring whether collaboration then reduces its
hallucination or amplifies it.

## 7 Ethical Considerations

All clinical text in this study comes from credentialed
PhysioNet [Goldberger et al. (2000)](#bib.bib39) datasets of
de-identified records — EHRNoteQA and Hallucinations-MIMIC-DI, both
derived from MIMIC-IV — and was used under their data use agreements by
credentialed researchers. MedExpQA, the retrieval corpus and the
open-weight models are publicly accessible and were used under their
released terms. Open-weight models, including the judge, were served on
local hardware, so the evaluation pipeline sent no clinical text outside
our infrastructure. The one exception is GPT-5.4-mini, which received
clinical text through the OpenAI API under zero data retention.

This is an evaluation study, not a deployment: nothing in it endorses
using these systems in clinical care, and the finding that collaboration
can increase hallucination argues for caution. Our measures are also
reference-relative proxies, so a low hallucination rate is not evidence
that a system’s reasoning is safe to act on. We release the code for
every experiment; it contains scripts only and no data.

## Appendix A System Prompts

Figure [8](#A1.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix A System Prompts ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
gives every role’s prompt exactly as in the configuration the runs used.
Each topology is instantiated identically for every model, so the
scaffold is held constant and only the model changes. MIMIC-DI detection
asks the system to annotate a summary against its source rather than to
answer a question, so there each role’s prompt is replaced by a
task-adapted one (right column); the topology, its size and every
setting in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Inference Settings ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
are unchanged.

|                     |                    |
| ------------------- | ------------------ |
| MedExpQA, EHRNoteQA | MIMIC-DI detection |

SLS solver  You are a careful medical expert. Read the task and answer
it directly and precisely. solver  You are a meticulous clinical
fact-checker. You are given a doctor’s Brief Hospital Course (BHC), the
ONLY source of truth, and a patient discharge summary. Identify every
statement in the summary that the BHC does not support, following the
task instructions exactly. Return ONLY the requested JSON.

Panel specialists  (i) You are a diagnostician on a medical review
panel. Focus on differential diagnosis and clinical presentation; flag
any diagnostic reasoning that is unsupported or inconsistent with the
findings. (ii) You are a pharmacist on a medical review panel. Focus on
medication names, dosages, routes, and interactions; flag any
medication-related claim that is inaccurate or unsupported. (iii) You
are a general clinical fact-checker on a medical review panel. Verify
the claim against established medical knowledge and flag any factual,
procedural, or terminological error. specialists  (i) You are a
diagnostician on a clinical fact-checking panel. Scrutinize the summary
for unsupported diagnoses, symptoms, and clinical findings versus the
BHC. Report unsupported spans in the exact JSON format the task
requests. (ii) You are a pharmacist on a clinical fact-checking panel.
Scrutinize the summary for unsupported medications, doses, routes, and
frequencies versus the BHC. Report unsupported spans in the exact JSON
format the task requests. (iii) You are a general clinical fact-checker
on a panel. Scrutinize the summary for any procedure, time, location,
number, name, or wording unsupported by the BHC. Report unsupported
spans in the exact JSON format the task requests. moderator  You are the
moderator of a medical review panel. You are given a query and the
independent opinions of 3 specialists. Adopt only conclusions that AT
LEAST 2 of the 3 specialists independently support; discard any point
only a single specialist raised. Then give a single final answer in the
exact format requested by the original query. moderator  You are the
lead reviewer finalizing the panel’s hallucination annotation. You are
given the task and three colleagues’ annotation lists. Keep in the final
list ONLY spans that AT LEAST 2 of the 3 colleagues independently
flagged; DROP any span that only a single colleague flagged (treat lone
flags as false positives). Return ONLY the JSON object in the exact
format the task requests.

Debate debater  You are a careful medical expert. Read the task and
state your answer, with brief reasoning for it. debater  You are a
careful clinical fact-checker. Given the BHC (the only source of truth)
and the discharge summary, identify every unsupported statement
following the task instructions. Return ONLY the requested JSON.
revision turn  Here are the other debating agents’ current answers and
reasoning: {others} Reconsider your answer in light of these other
viewpoints. State your updated answer, with brief reasoning for it.
revision turn  Here are other fact-checkers’ annotations of the same
summary: {others} Reconsider your own annotation in light of theirs:
keep only spans genuinely unsupported by the BHC, add any true errors
you missed, and drop false positives. Return ONLY the requested JSON.
aggregator  You are the final decision maker. You are given the original
query and the debating agents’ final positions. Weigh them, resolve
disagreements, and give a single final answer in the exact format
requested by the original query. aggregator  You are the lead reviewer
finalizing the hallucination annotation. You are given the task and the
debaters’ final annotation lists. Merge them into ONE final annotation
list — keep every genuinely unsupported span, drop false positives and
duplicates. Return ONLY the JSON object the task requests.

Hierarchical proposers  (i) You are a careful medical expert. Reason
step by step from first principles, then answer the question directly
and precisely. (ii) You are a meticulous medical fact-checker.
Cross-check the claim against established clinical guidelines, then
answer the question directly and precisely. (iii) You are an experienced
clinician who prioritizes patient safety. Note any uncertainty, then
answer the question directly and precisely. proposers  (i) You are a
clinical fact-checker focused on unsupported diagnoses and findings.
Annotate the summary against the BHC per the task instructions. Return
ONLY the requested JSON. (ii) You are a clinical fact-checker focused on
unsupported medications, procedures, and numbers. Annotate the summary
against the BHC per the task instructions. Return ONLY the requested
JSON. (iii) You are a clinical fact-checker focused on unsupported
names, times, locations, and wording. Annotate the summary against the
BHC per the task instructions. Return ONLY the requested JSON.
refinement layer  Here is the original query and candidate answers to it
from a previous round of independent experts: Original query: {query}
Previous answers: {others} Using these as reference, give your own
improved answer to the original query, in the exact format it requests.
refinement layer  Here is the fact-checking task and candidate
annotations from a previous round of fact-checkers: Original request:
{query} Previous annotations: {others} Using these as reference, produce
your own improved annotation — keep only genuinely unsupported spans,
add missed true errors, and drop false positives. Return ONLY the
requested JSON. aggregator  You are the final decision maker. You are
given the original query and several independent experts’ proposed
answers. Synthesize them into a single best answer, resolving any
disagreements, and answer the original query in the exact format it
requests. aggregator  You are the lead reviewer finalizing the
hallucination annotation. You are given the task and several
fact-checkers’ annotation lists. Merge them into ONE final annotation
list — keep every genuinely unsupported span, drop false positives and
duplicates. Return ONLY the JSON object the task requests.

Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Inference Settings ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

## Appendix B Inference Settings

Every setting below is held constant across all models, topologies and
tasks, so that a difference in results is attributable to the system and
not to how it was run.

#### Generation.

Temperature $`0.7`$ on every turn of every topology. The two follow-up
experiments regenerate a single call per item at temperature $`0`$ with
output capped at $`2{,}048`$ tokens: the aggregator call in the
aggregator swap
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"))
and the rewrite in the self-correction experiment
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Self-Correction Capability and Multi-Agent Collaboration ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
Context budget $`8{,}192`$ prompt tokens per agent turn, truncated
oldest-first while keeping the system message. Output capped at
$`4{,}096`$ tokens per turn. Reasoning traces are stripped before
parsing and before being passed to another agent. No factuality or
consistency directive is appended to any prompt: the systems are run as
specified in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A System Prompts ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
and nothing else.

#### Reasoning.

Hybrid-reasoning models are run with reasoning off, so that all models
are compared in the same mode.

#### Serving.

Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct are served with vLLM in bfloat16 at
$`0.92`$ GPU memory utilization, $`16{,}384`$ maximum model length and
$`64`$ concurrent sequences; tensor parallelism is set per model to fit
its weights. DeepSeek-V4.1-flash is also served from its open weights
with vLLM, in its released FP8/FP4 precision; GPT-5.4-mini is called
through the OpenAI API. The serving context is twice the harness budget
so that truncation is performed by the harness, not by the server.

#### Judge.

All judging uses one local open-weight model, gemma-4-31B-it, at
temperature $`0.0`$. Claim decomposition is capped at $`1{,}200`$ output
tokens, per-claim classification at $`300`$, and the two
logical-inconsistency steps at $`160`$ (each pair alone) and $`900`$
(resolution with the source). Retrieval for the factuality axis is BM25
over $`346{,}691`$ MedRAG textbook and StatPearls passages at
$`k{=}20`$. No external API is used anywhere in the evaluation pipeline.

#### Computing environment.

Qwen3-32B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and the judge run on a shared academic
cluster under SLURM, on NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs: Qwen3-32B and the
judge at tensor parallelism $`2`$, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct on a single GPU
(its main generation run on one NVIDIA A16). They are served with vLLM
0.19.0 on PyTorch 2.10 (CUDA 12.8). Retrieval uses bm25s 0.3.11; the
bootstrap, $`\kappa`$ and AC1 are computed with our own NumPy code.
DeepSeek-V4.1-flash requires vLLM 0.31.0 and more GPU memory, so its
generation runs use a separate secured server with NVIDIA H200 NVL GPUs
(tensor parallelism $`4`$, its Engram memory offloaded to the CPU, as in
the vLLM recipe for this model); its self-correction rewrites use the
same configuration on the cluster’s H200 NVL GPUs and are judged there.
Its main-run outputs are judged on the same server, on two H200 GPUs, by
the same judge model and revision in an exact copy of the cluster’s vLLM
0.19.0 environment. DeepSeek-V4.1-flash’s outputs are the only ones
judged on different hardware, which matters because temperature-$`0`$
judgments are not bit-identical across GPU types. No clinical text
leaves these two machines except the GPT-5.4-mini calls, which use the
OpenAI API under zero data retention.

## Appendix C Task Definitions

Table [C](#A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1 "MedExpQA retrieval. ‣ Appendix C Task Definitions ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
lists, for each task, the metric we report, the hallucination sub-types
it exercises, what the system is given, and what its rationale is judged
against. All three tasks are in English. The $`200`$ MedExpQA items are
drawn from its $`622`$ English items, stratified by specialty; the
$`200`$ EHRNoteQA questions are drawn from its level-1 questions,
stratified by the number of notes; both draws use a fixed seed. MIMIC-DI
uses all $`200`$ annotated summaries, $`100`$ model-generated and
$`100`$ written by clinicians.

#### MedExpQA retrieval.

MedExpQA also ships retrieval passages for each question, but we check
claims against our own corpus
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Hallucination Evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
In a pilot on $`336`$ claims the gold explanation leaves open,
retrieving from our corpus for each claim settled $`68\%`$ of them,
against $`42\%`$ with the shipped passages, confirming and refuting more
claims alike.

## Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment

#### Procedure.

The experiment starts from the judged single-agent rationales of the
main run
(§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Hallucination Evaluation ‣ 3 Experimental Setup ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).
From each, we take the flags the paper counts: claims labeled factual
contradiction or fabrication on MedExpQA; on EHRNoteQA and MIMIC-DI,
claims that contradict the source document (a claim the source merely
does not state is not fed back), and the contradicting pairs of the
logical-inconsistency judge. Items with none of these are not re-run and
enter the comparison unchanged. For every other item, the same model
answers the same item again, with the original task prompt followed by a
block headed “errors found in a previous attempt at this exact item”.
The block lists each flagged MedExpQA statement with its error type and
the reference it was judged against: for a contradiction, the passage it
contradicts (from the gold explanation or a retrieved textbook passage);
for a fabrication, that no support was found in either. The full gold
explanation is not shown, since it names the answer. Contextual flags
are listed as statements that contradict the source document, and
logical flags as pairs of statements that cannot both be true of the
patient. The block ends: “Be aware of these errors. Do not repeat them.
Answer the item again”, and asks that every statement be medically
accurate, consistent with the source document, or free of contradiction,
according to the flags shown. The model does not see its previous
rationale, only the flagged statements. The rewrite is generated at
temperature $`0`$ with output capped at $`2{,}048`$ tokens
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Inference Settings ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")),
and judged by the same pipeline and judge model as every other output.
For DeepSeek-V4.1-flash, the rewrites are generated with the same
serving configuration as its main run, on the cluster’s own H200 NVL
GPUs, and judged there
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Inference Settings ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")).

#### Measure.

For each sub-type, the before and after rates are the per-claim rates of
the original and the rewrite, computed per item and averaged over items,
the aggregation used throughout the paper; for logical inconsistency the
rate is the share of claims that take part in a contradicting pair. The
net change is the difference, with a $`95\%`$ bootstrap interval over
items ($`2{,}000`$ resamples). The population is every single-agent
rationale with at least one claim, as for the rates in
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Hallucination Category Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"),
so before matches them except on MIMIC-DI, where some rewrites flag no
span and so contain no claim ($`10`$ for DeepSeek-V4.1-flash, $`11`$ for
Qwen3-32B, $`25`$ for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct); like a single-agent
rationale with no claim, they have no rate and are left out of both
before and after.
Table [6](#A6.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Logical inconsistency. ‣ Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
gives the levels behind
Figure [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.3 Scaling Agents and Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?").

#### Ordering.

Averaged over factual contradiction, fabrication and contextual
inconsistency, the net change after correction is $`-0.025`$ for
GPT-5.4-mini, $`-0.018`$ for DeepSeek-V4.1-flash, $`-0.007`$ for
Qwen3-32B and $`+0.003`$ for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Averaged over the
nine system–task comparisons of
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?"),
collaboration changes hallucination by $`-0.011`$, $`+0.002`$,
$`+0.013`$ and $`+0.017`$ respectively. The two orderings are identical
(Spearman $`1.00`$); with four models this is the best of $`24`$
possible arrangements ($`p=0.042`$), which establishes the order but not
the strength of the relationship.

#### Logical inconsistency.

Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Logical inconsistency. ‣ Appendix F Self-Correction Experiment ‣ Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?")
counts contradicting pairs rather than rates, separating the items whose
prompt showed a contradiction from those re-run only for other errors,
where every pair in the rewrite is new. No claim alignment is involved.
Shown its contradictions, every model removes most of them. On items
re-run for other errors, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct writes $`29`$ new pairs
over $`180`$ items ($`0.16`$ per item), against $`9`$ over $`158`$ for
GPT-5.4-mini ($`0.06`$), $`9`$ over $`114`$ for DeepSeek-V4.1-flash
($`0.08`$) and $`13`$ over $`136`$ for Qwen3-32B ($`0.10`$). On
EHRNoteQA, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct’s new pairs outweigh the ones it
removes, and its contradictions rise from $`17`$ pairs to $`25`$.
